## Today's Agenda

1. Why coding systems matter: from raw data to **phenotypes**
2. The major coding systems: **ICD, CPT, LOINC, SNOMED CT**
3. Hierarchies: how codes relate to each other
4. The **OMOP Common Data Model** and standardized vocabularies (**Athena**)
5. Korean adaptations: **KCD, EDI, K-OMOP**
6. Hands-on: querying a mock vocabulary hierarchy in R
7. Reference websites for code look-up

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Distinguish diagnosis codes (ICD), procedure codes (CPT/HCPCS), lab/observation codes (LOINC), and clinical terminology (SNOMED CT)
- Explain why hierarchical structure matters for defining phenotypes
- Describe the role of the OMOP CDM and its standardized vocabularies
- Navigate Athena to look up a concept and its ancestors/descendants
- Describe how Korean vocabularies (KCD, EDI) are mapped into OMOP

# 1. From Codes to Phenotypes

## Why This Matters

Electronic health records and claims data are **coded** as structured data, not written in free text (mostly).

Free text from progress notes require NLP/LLMs - considered separately.

> A **phenotype** is an operational definition of a clinical concept (e.g., "Type 2 Diabetes") built from combinations of codes, values, and rules applied to structured data.

- Codes are the atoms; phenotypes are the molecules
- Getting the codes and hierarchy right makes a more valid and less biased cohort
- Multi-site / multi-country research (e.g., US + Korea) requires **mapping** between local and international vocabularies

## The Landscape

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Patient Encounter] --> B[Diagnosis\nICD-10 / ICD-10-CM / KCD]
  A --> C[Procedure\nCPT / HCPCS / EDI]
  A --> D[Lab / Observation\nLOINC]
  A --> E[Clinical finding\nSNOMED CT]
  B --> F[(OMOP CDM\nStandardized Vocabularies)]
  C --> F
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F --> G[Computable Phenotype /\nCohort Definition]
```

# 2. Major Coding Systems

## ICD — International Classification of Diseases

- Maintained by **WHO**; primary use: diagnoses, mortality statistics, reimbursement
- Key versions:
  - **ICD-9-CM** — legacy, US, retired for most uses
  - **ICD-10** — WHO version, used internationally for mortality/morbidity
  - **ICD-10-CM** — US clinical modification, much more granular
  - **ICD-11** — current WHO version, fully hierarchical, multi-axial
- Structure: category + etiology/anatomic site/severity/laterality + extension
- Example: `E11.9` = Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications

## ICD Hierarchy Example

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["Chapter IV: Endocrine, nutritional,\nand metabolic diseases (E00-E90)"] --> B["E08-E13: Diabetes mellitus"]
  B --> C["E11: Type 2 diabetes mellitus"]
  C --> D["E11.9: ...without complications"]
  C --> E["E11.2-: ...with kidney complications"]
  C --> F["E11.3-: ...with ophthalmic complications"]
```

A **phenotype algorithm** for "Type 2 Diabetes" may use `E11.*` parent plus all descendants

## CPT — Current Procedural Terminology

- Maintained by the **American Medical Association (AMA)**
- Describes **what was done**: procedures, services, surgeries
- 5-digit numeric codes, organized into categories:
  - Category I: routine clinical procedures (e.g., `99213` office visit)
  - Category II: performance measurement (optional, alphanumeric)
  - Category III: emerging/experimental technology (temporary codes)
- Often paired with **HCPCS Level II** codes (supplies, drugs, DME) in US claims data
- CPT is **proprietary/licensed** — unlike ICD or LOINC

Examples: 90999 for dialysis in facility, and S9339 for peritoneal dialysis at home

## LOINC — Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes

- Maintained by the **Regenstrief Institute**
- Standardizes **lab tests, clinical measurements, and observations**
- Each code is defined by **six axes**:

| Axis | Example |
|---|---|
| Component | Glucose |
| Property | Mass concentration |
| Timing | Point in time |
| System | Serum/Plasma |
| Scale | Quantitative |
| Method | (optional, e.g., "test strip") |

- Example: `2345-7` = Glucose \[Mass/volume\] in Serum or Plasma (random)

## SNOMED CT

- Maintained by **SNOMED International**; most comprehensive clinical terminology
- Covers diagnoses, findings, procedures, body structures, organisms, and more 
- Concepts are linked by **formal relationships**, not just hierarchy:
  - `Is a` (hierarchical parent/child)
  - `Finding site`, `Causative agent`, `Associated morphology`, etc.

Example: "Bacterial pneumonia" 

- Is a: Pneumonia
- Is a: Bacterial infectious disease
- Finding site: Lung structure
- Causative agent: Bacterium
- Associated morphology: Inflammation

## SNOMED CT "Is a" Hierarchy Example

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["Clinical finding"] --> B["Disease"]
  B --> C["Disorder of endocrine system"]
  C --> D["Disorder of glucose metabolism"]
  D --> E["Diabetes mellitus"]
  E --> F["Type 2 diabetes mellitus"]
  F --> G["Type 2 diabetes mellitus\nwith diabetic nephropathy"]
```

Each concept can also carry defining attributes, e.g. `Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic nephropathy` → `Associated morphology = Nephropathy`, `Finding site = Kidney structure`.

# 3. Hierarchies in Practice

## Why Hierarchy Matters for Phenotyping

- Clinicians *rarely* code with a single, most-specific term consistently
- A phenotype for "diabetes" likely needs **all descendants** of the diabetes concept
- Two core hierarchy operations:
  - **Ancestors**: broader/parent concepts 
  - **Descendants**: narrower/child concepts

## A Tiny Mock Hierarchy in R

```{r}
#| label: mock-hierarchy
# A minimal parent-child edge list, similar in spirit to
# OMOP's concept_ancestor table (but built by hand here)
edges <- tibble::tribble(
  ~parent,                     ~child,
  "Diabetes mellitus",         "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",
  "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",  "T2DM without complications",
  "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",  "T2DM with nephropathy",
  "T2DM with nephropathy",     "T2DM with nephropathy, stage 3 CKD"
)

edges
```

# 4. The OMOP Common Data Model

## What Is OMOP CDM?

- **OMOP** = Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership; the data model is now stewarded by **OHDSI** (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics)
- A relational schema that any clinical/claims dataset can be transformed (ETL) into tables
- Core clinical tables: `person`, `condition_occurrence`, `drug_exposure`, `procedure_occurrence`, `measurement`, `observation`, `visit_occurrence`
- Every clinical fact is expressed using a **standard concept_id**, regardless of the source vocabulary

## Standard vs. Source Concepts

- Every code from ICD, CPT, LOINC, KCD, EDI, etc. becomes a row in the `concept` table
- Each concept has a `standard_concept` flag:
  - `"S"` — Standard: concept to use for analysis
  - `NULL`/blank — Non-standard: kept for traceability, mapped to a standard concept
  - `"C"` — Classification concept (used for grouping, not for analyses)
- Non-standard source codes are linked to standard concepts via a `"Maps to"` relationship

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Source code\ne.g. ICD-10-CM E11.9\n(non-standard)"] -- "Maps to" --> B["Standard concept\nSNOMED CT: Type 2 diabetes mellitus"]
  B -- "Is a" --> C["Ancestor concept\nDiabetes mellitus"]
```

## Key OMOP Vocabulary Tables

| Table | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `concept` | One row per code/term across all vocabularies |
| `vocabulary` | Registry of vocabularies (ICD10CM, LOINC, SNOMED, KCD7, EDI, ...) |
| `concept_relationship` | Pairwise relationships, e.g. "Maps to", "Is a" |
| `concept_ancestor` | *All* ancestor–descendant pairs (with levels of separation) |
| `domain` | Which table a concept belongs to (Condition, Drug, Procedure...) |

## Athena: The OHDSI Vocabulary Browser

- **Athena** (<https://athena.ohdsi.org>) hosts every vocabulary OHDSI supports — ICD, CPT4, LOINC, SNOMED CT, RxNorm, etc.
- Typical workflow:
  1. Search a term or code
  2. Inspect its domain, standard/non-standard status, and vocabulary
  3. View **relationships** ("Maps to", "Is a") and **hierarchy** (ancestors/descendants)
  4. Download a full vocabulary snapshot (CSV) for local work if needed

# 5. Phenotyping with Coded Data

## A Computable Phenotype

A "Type 2 Diabetes" cohort might be defined as:

> Patients with **≥2 condition_occurrence records** mapped to any **descendant of concept_id 1002** (T2DM) that are **standard concepts**, **at least 30 days apart**, OR **≥1 record plus a diabetes drug exposure**

## Phenotype Libraries & Tools

- **OHDSI ATLAS** (<https://atlas-demo.ohdsi.org>) — web tool to build, share, and run cohort definitions across sites without sharing patient data
- **OHDSI Phenotype Library** — community-vetted, validated phenotype definitions
- **PheKB** (<https://phekb.org>) — algorithms combining codes, labs, and NLP for phenotyping
- Good practice: always version and document your code sets (which vocabulary version, which concept_ids, which logic)

# 6. Korean Adaptations

## KCD — Korean Standard Classification of Diseases

- Built on **ICD-10**, extended for Korean healthcare system
- Used for medical records, cause-of-death statistics, and insurance claims
- Current edition: **KCD-9**
- Look-up: KOICD portal — <https://www.koicd.kr/kcd/kcds.do>
- In OMOP, `KCD7`/`KCD8` are loaded as **non-standard** vocabularies, and `"Maps to"` **SNOMED CT** standard concepts

## EDI Codes — Korea's Claims/Procedure Vocabulary

- From **HIRA** for national health insurance reimbursement
- Cover procedures, medical services, devices, and drugs used in claims, similar to **CPT + HCPCS** in the US
- The **full EDI code set has been incorporated into the OMOP vocabulary** (via Athena)
- EDI concepts are loaded as **non-standard**; map to standard concepts for analysis

## Korean OMOP CDM Networks (K-OMOP)

- Korea has one of the most active **OHDSI communities** outside the US (**K-OHDSI**)
- National-scale conversions to OMOP CDM:
  - **HIRA K-OMOP** — nationwide claims data converted to OMOP by mapping EDI → OMOP standard concepts
  - Multiple university hospitals and NHIS-linked databases participate in **multi-site OHDSI network studies**
- Korean data be analyzed with the **same R/ATLAS tools** used elsewhere

- **OHDSI Korea (K-OHDSI)** forum posts on EDI/KCD integration: <https://forums.ohdsi.org/>

## Summary

- Diagnoses (**ICD/KCD**), procedures (**CPT/EDI**), labs (**LOINC**), and clinical concepts (**SNOMED CT**) have different purposes and structures
- Hierarchy (parent/child, ancestor/descendant) turns single code into usable **phenotype definition**
- **OMOP CDM + Athena** unify into one queryable structure, distinguishing **standard** vs. **source** concepts
- Korea's **KCD** and **EDI** vocabularies are now integrated into OMOP/Athena, for **Korean data to plug into international network research** with the same R tools
